stages.title: Decide and name
stages.blurb: Pick the structure, check the name, know your taxes before you file anything.

stages.title: Register the entity
stages.blurb: Incorporation or the proprietor’s minimum proofs.

stages.title: Tax identities
stages.blurb: PAN, TAN, GST — the numbers every invoice and bank form will ask for.

stages.title: Licences and registrations
stages.blurb: Udyam, Shops & Establishment, FSSAI, trademark and the sector-specific permits.

stages.title: Banking and payments
stages.blurb: Current account, UPI, payment gateway, invoicing.

stages.title: Selling setup
stages.blurb: Store, marketplaces, labels, policies and consumer-law duties.

stages.title: Import and export
stages.blurb: IEC, AD code, customs, LUT, realisation and incentives.

stages.title: Going international
stages.blurb: Foreign payments, subsidiaries abroad, foreign investors.

stages.title: Run and stay compliant
stages.blurb: Books, returns, audits and the annual calendar.

steps.title: Choose the legal structure
steps.why: The structure fixes your liability, tax rate, compliance load and whether investors can buy in. Changing later costs money and time.
steps.how: Solo and small: proprietorship (fastest, personal liability). Partners: LLP (limited liability, 30% tax, light filings). Raising money or building a brand: private limited (investor-ready, 25.17% tax option, audited every year). Use the structure tool, then read the guide.

steps.title: Check the name — MCA, trademark, domain, handles
steps.why: A name that clashes with an existing company, LLP or trademark gets rejected or, worse, works for a year and then draws a cease-and-desist.
steps.how: Search MCA company/LLP master data, the IP India trademark public search (same and similar classes), the .in/.com domain and Instagram/X handles. Shortlist three names.

steps.title: Identify your HSN/SAC codes and NIC code
steps.why: GST rate, e-way bills, import duty, Udyam and incorporation forms all key off these codes. Wrong codes mean wrong tax.
steps.how: Find the HSN (goods) or SAC (services) on the GST rate finder; for imports use the 8-digit ITC-HS on ICEGATE. Pick the 5-digit NIC 2008 code for your activity (needed in SPICe+ and Udyam).

steps.title: Write a founders’ agreement (equity, vesting, roles, exit)
steps.why: Most startup failures that end in court began with an undocumented 50:50 handshake.
steps.how: Agree ownership, vesting (typically 4 years, 1-year cliff), decision rights, IP assignment to the company, what happens if someone leaves. Fold it into the LLP agreement or the shareholders’ agreement.

steps.title: Get Class 3 Digital Signature Certificates for every director/partner
steps.why: Every MCA, GST and DGFT filing is signed digitally. Nothing moves without a DSC.
steps.how: Buy from a CCA-licensed certifying authority (eMudhra, Sify, Capricorn, etc.) with PAN, Aadhaar, photo and video verification; it arrives on a USB token or as a download.

steps.title: Incorporate the company with SPICe+ (Part A name, Part B incorporation)
steps.why: One web form on MCA V3 reserves the name and issues the Certificate of Incorporation, PAN, TAN, and (via AGILE-PRO-S) EPFO, ESIC, profession-tax and bank-account applications together.
steps.how: Part A: propose up to two names (₹1,000). Within 20 days, Part B: directors (DIN allotted for up to three new directors), registered office proof, e-MoA and e-AoA, INC-9 declaration, AGILE-PRO-S. Pay stamp duty (state-wise). Certificate usually within 7–15 working days.
steps.cost: MCA fee nil up to ₹15 lakh authorised capital + ₹1,000 name + state stamp duty (₹500–10,000+) + professional fee ₹5,000–15,000
docs: PAN and Aadhaar of each director and subscriber
Address proof (bank statement/utility bill under 2 months)
Registered-office proof: utility bill + rent agreement/NOC from owner

steps.title: Incorporate the LLP with FiLLiP and file the LLP agreement (Form 3)
steps.why: FiLLiP reserves the name, allots DPINs and issues the certificate; the LLP agreement filed within 30 days is what actually governs profit shares and decisions.
steps.how: File RUN-LLP or name within FiLLiP, then FiLLiP with partner details and registered-office proof. Within 30 days of incorporation, execute the LLP agreement on stamp paper (state duty) and file Form 3. Apply for PAN/TAN alongside.
steps.cost: ₹500–5,000 MCA fee by contribution + stamp duty + professional fee ₹4,000–10,000
docs: PAN, Aadhaar, photo of each partner

steps.title: Execute and register the partnership deed
steps.why: Unregistered partnerships cannot sue third parties or partners to enforce rights; registration with the state Registrar of Firms fixes that and banks ask for it.
steps.how: Draft the deed (capital, profit ratio, duties, admission/retirement), notarise on stamp paper, apply to the state Registrar of Firms with Form 1, then get the firm’s PAN.
docs: PAN and address proof of partners

steps.title: Create the proprietor’s business proofs (Udyam, GST or Shops & Establishment)
steps.why: A proprietorship has no incorporation certificate; banks, marketplaces and payment gateways accept any two of Udyam, GSTIN or a Shops & Establishment certificate as proof the business exists.
steps.how: Register on Udyam (free, instant) and either take GST (if you need it anyway) or the state Shops & Establishment registration. Use your personal PAN for everything.
steps.cost: Free (Udyam, GST); S&E fee ₹100–5,000 by state

steps.title: File INC-20A (commencement of business) within 180 days
steps.why: A company cannot start business or borrow until subscribers have paid for their shares and INC-20A is filed; late filing attracts ₹50,000 on the company plus ₹1,000/day on directors.
steps.how: Open the current account, have each subscriber transfer the share money, then file INC-20A with the bank statement as proof.

steps.title: Fix the registered office and display the name board
steps.why: The registered office receives legal notices; the name, CIN/LLPIN, address, phone and GSTIN must be displayed outside and on letterheads and invoices.
steps.how: A home address works for a company or LLP (owner NOC). Put a board at the entrance with name, address and CIN; print letterheads with CIN, registered office and email.

steps.title: Get the entity PAN and TAN
steps.why: PAN identifies the business for every tax and bank; TAN is needed to deduct and deposit TDS on salaries, rent, contractors and professionals.
steps.how: Companies and LLPs get PAN and TAN inside SPICe+/FiLLiP. Partnerships apply via Protean (Form 49A/49B). Proprietors use their own PAN and apply for TAN only when they start deducting TDS.

steps.title: Decide whether GST registration is mandatory, optional or worth taking voluntarily
steps.why: Below ₹40 lakh (goods) / ₹20 lakh (services) it is optional — unless you sell inter-state goods, sell through a marketplace, import, export under LUT or want input credit. Registering too early adds monthly filings; too late invites penalties.
steps.how: Run the GST checker. Marketplaces generally require a GSTIN; exporters need one to file a LUT and claim refunds; B2B customers want to claim credit on your invoice.

steps.title: Register for GST (REG-01) with Aadhaar authentication
steps.why: You cannot collect GST, claim input credit, sell on most marketplaces or export zero-rated without a GSTIN.
steps.how: On the GST portal: Part A (PAN, mobile, email), Part B (business details, promoters, principal place of business with proof, bank, HSN/SAC). Complete Aadhaar OTP or, if flagged, biometric verification at a GST Suvidha Kendra. Rule 14A (output tax ≤ ₹2.5 lakh/month) gives approval in 3 working days; otherwise 7 working days, or 30 with physical verification. Add bank details within 30 days.
docs: Proof of principal place of business: electricity bill/property tax + rent agreement or NOC
Board resolution or authorisation letter for the signatory
Bank statement or cancelled cheque (within 30 days)

steps.title: Pick regular vs composition vs QRMP filing
steps.why: Composition (turnover ≤ ₹1.5 crore) means one quarterly payment and no input credit; regular taxpayers under ₹5 crore can file quarterly returns with monthly payments (QRMP). The choice changes cash flow and what you can sell.
steps.how: Composition suits local B2C traders and restaurants with low input credit; it bars inter-state sales and most marketplace selling. Everyone else: regular, with QRMP if under ₹5 crore and you prefer quarterly GSTR-1/3B.
steps.time: 15 minutes (opt in before the year starts)

steps.title: File a Letter of Undertaking (RFD-11) to export without paying IGST
steps.why: Exports are zero-rated; without a LUT you must pay IGST on every export invoice and claim it back months later.
steps.how: On the GST portal, Services → Refunds → Furnish LUT, each financial year before your first export (renew every April). Two witnesses, no bank guarantee for non-defaulters.

steps.title: Register on Udyam (MSME)
steps.why: Free and instant; unlocks priority-sector lending, CGTMSE guarantees, 45-day payment protection, 50% off trademark fees, tender exemptions and several state subsidies. Also a business proof for proprietors.
steps.how: Aadhaar of the proprietor/partner/director + PAN (+ GSTIN where registered). Self-declare investment and turnover; the portal pulls ITR and GST data later.

steps.title: Register under the state Shops and Establishments Act
steps.why: Most states require every shop, office, warehouse or commercial establishment to register within 30 days of opening; it also doubles as a business proof for banks.
steps.how: Apply on your state labour department portal (or via the state single window / AGILE-PRO-S for new companies in some states) with address proof, PAN, employee count and photos of the premises.

steps.title: Get the municipal trade licence (shops, eateries, workshops)
steps.why: Municipal corporations license physical trade premises; running a store or kitchen without one leads to sealing and fines.
steps.how: Apply to the municipal corporation/panchayat with premises proof, property tax receipt, NOC from the owner and, where applicable, fire NOC. Renew annually.
steps.cost: ₹500–10,000 a year by city and trade

steps.title: Get FSSAI registration or licence (FoSCoS)
steps.why: Every food business — home kitchen, cloud kitchen, café, packaged-food brand, importer, food e-commerce — must display a 14-digit FSSAI number. Platforms like Swiggy and Zomato will not onboard without it.
steps.how: Turnover up to ₹1.5 crore: Basic registration (₹100/yr). ₹1.5–50 crore: State licence (₹2,000–5,000/yr). Above ₹50 crore, importers and e-commerce food operators: Central licence (₹7,500/yr). Apply on FoSCoS with ID, premises proof and, for licences, a food-safety plan and layout.

steps.title: File the trademark (TM-A) for your brand name and logo
steps.why: A registered mark lets you stop copycats, join Amazon Brand Registry and licence the brand later. Filing early also lets you use ™ immediately.
steps.how: Pick the right Nice classes (e.g., 25 apparel, 35 retail/online, 42 software), run a public search, file TM-A online (₹4,500 per class for individuals/startups/MSMEs with Udyam or DPIIT certificate, ₹9,000 otherwise). Expect examination in 3–6 months and registration in 12–24 months.
docs: Udyam or DPIIT certificate for the concession
Power of attorney (TM-48) if using an agent
User affidavit if claiming prior use

steps.title: Apply for DPIIT Startup India recognition
steps.why: Free recognition unlocks the 3-year tax holiday application, self-certification under labour and environment laws, 80% patent and 50% trademark rebates, public-procurement relaxations and access to the Seed Fund and Fund of Funds.
steps.how: On NSWS add the “Registration as a Startup” form: incorporation certificate, a write-up on innovation/scalability, website or pitch deck. Private limited, LLP, registered partnership or cooperative; under 10 years old; turnover under ₹200 crore. Certificate in roughly 1–3 weeks.
steps.cost: Free — nobody is authorised to charge for it

steps.title: Comply with the Legal Metrology Packaged Commodities Rules (labels and LMPC registration)
steps.why: Every pre-packed product sold in India must declare manufacturer/packer/importer name and address, common name, net quantity, MRP inclusive of all taxes, month/year of manufacture or import, consumer-care details and country of origin for imports — on the pack and, from 2027, searchably online.
steps.how: Design the principal display panel to Rule 6; manufacturers/packers register with the state Controller of Legal Metrology and importers with the Director (Rule 27) before the first consignment. Marketplaces show these declarations on the listing.

steps.title: Check BIS: ISI mark, CRS for electronics, hallmarking and Quality Control Orders
steps.why: Over 700 products (electronics under CRS, toys, steel, cement, footwear, some textiles) cannot be sold or imported without BIS certification; customs holds non-compliant shipments.
steps.how: Search the product on bis.gov.in and the QCO list. For imports, the foreign factory must hold the BIS licence/registration. Budget 8–16 weeks and lab testing in India.
steps.cost: ₹25,000–several lakh depending on product and tests

steps.title: Factory licence, pollution consents (CTE/CTO) and fire NOC for manufacturing
steps.why: Manufacturing units need Consent to Establish before construction and Consent to Operate before production from the State Pollution Control Board; factories with 10+ workers (power) or 20+ (no power) need a Factory Licence; fire NOC for most premises above thresholds.
steps.how: Classify the unit as White/Green/Orange/Red on the SPCB portal (White needs only an intimation). Apply for CTE, then CTO; Factory licence from the Chief Inspector of Factories with building plan approval; fire NOC from the state fire service. State single windows bundle these.

steps.title: Sector licence check: drugs/cosmetics (CDSCO), liquor, insurance/finance (RBI/IRDAI/SEBI), education, telecom, security
steps.why: Regulated sectors need a licence before day one, and the licence often dictates the structure (e.g., NBFCs must be companies with ₹10 crore net owned funds).
steps.how: Match your product to the regulator: cosmetics and devices → CDSCO manufacturing/import licence; nutraceuticals → FSSAI plus product approval; lending or payment aggregation → RBI; brokerage/advisory → SEBI; drones → DGCA; private security → PSARA. When unsure, ask the regulator’s helpdesk in writing.

steps.title: Open a current account in the business name
steps.why: Keeps business money separate (essential for books, GST reconciliation and audits) and is required for payment gateways, marketplaces and INC-20A.
steps.how: Companies/LLPs: incorporation certificate, PAN, MoA/AoA or LLP agreement, board resolution, KYC of signatories. Proprietors: PAN, Aadhaar plus two business proofs (Udyam, GSTIN, Shops & Establishment). Compare monthly average balance requirements and payout fees; new-age banks and neobanks on top of banks are fine.
steps.cost: ₹0–10,000 average balance; some zero-balance for startups
docs: Board resolution or partners’ authority letter

steps.title: Set up UPI, a payment gateway and invoicing software
steps.why: You need to collect money compliantly and issue GST-compliant invoices from the first sale.
steps.how: Merchant UPI QR from your bank or a PA (Razorpay, Cashfree, PayU, PhonePe PG, Paytm); gateway onboarding needs PAN, bank proof, business proof and a website with terms, privacy, refund and contact pages. Pick accounting software with GST filing and an audit trail (Zoho Books, Tally Prime, Vyapar, Busy).

steps.title: Arrange to receive foreign currency with purpose codes and FIRA/e-BRC
steps.why: Export income must land in an Indian bank with the right purpose code and be documented (FIRA/e-FIRC, e-BRC) within the RBI realisation period, or the money is a FEMA problem rather than revenue.
steps.how: Use your AD bank’s SWIFT details, or a cross-border PA (Razorpay International, Skydo, Xflow, PayPal, Payoneer) that auto-issues FIRAs. Stripe India is invite-only. Quote invoices in foreign currency with your IEC and LUT number.
steps.cost: 0.5–4% of each receipt plus FX spread

steps.title: Publish the legally required pages: terms, privacy, refunds/returns, shipping, contact, grievance officer
steps.why: Payment gateways reject sites without them; the IT Rules, Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules and DPDP Act require privacy notices, a grievance officer and clear return terms.
steps.how: Write them in plain English (and Hindi if you sell to Bharat): what data you collect and why, how to withdraw consent, return/refund timelines, delivery promises, legal name and address, grievance officer name/email/phone with 48-hour acknowledgement.

steps.title: Onboard to marketplaces (Amazon, Flipkart, Meesho, Myntra, JioMart, quick commerce, ONDC)
steps.why: Marketplaces bring demand you cannot buy early, but they are tax collectors too: they deduct GST TCS (0.5%) and income-tax TDS (0.1%) and report every sale.
steps.how: Needs GSTIN (except exempt categories/some intra-state schemes), PAN, bank account, brand name or authorisation, product photos and GTIN/EAN barcodes for many categories. Register for Brand Registry with your trademark. Check fees per category (referral 2–20%, closing fee, shipping).
steps.cost: Free to list; commissions per sale; barcodes ₹2,000–5,000

steps.title: Launch your own store (Shopify, WooCommerce, Dukaan, Instamojo) with GST-compliant checkout
steps.why: Owning the customer relationship protects margins and data; but your store must compute GST per HSN, show MRP and tax-inclusive prices and issue invoices.
steps.how: Pick a platform with Indian payment gateways and GST invoicing; set tax rates by HSN; collect shipping and billing state for place-of-supply; integrate a shipping aggregator (Shiprocket, Delhivery, iThink).

steps.title: Open the physical store: lease, signage licence, POS billing, fire safety
steps.why: Besides Shops & Establishment and trade licence, a shop needs a registered lease, a signage/advertisement permission in many cities, a GST-ready POS and basic fire compliance.
steps.how: Register the lease (mandatory above 11 months), apply for the signboard licence at the municipal body, set up POS billing software that prints GST invoices, keep extinguishers and exits per fire rules, display FSSAI/GST/S&E certificates.

steps.title: Meet the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules — including the 2026 amendments from 1 Jan 2027
steps.why: Sellers must show legal name, address, GSTIN/Udyam, country of origin, best-before dates, return and return-shipping terms and warranty; discounts must reference the lowest price of the last 30 days; no fake reviews or dark patterns.
steps.how: Audit your listings and checkout against the rules; appoint a grievance officer (48-hour acknowledgement, 1-month resolution); keep price history to justify ‘was’ prices; label sponsored placements; do the annual dark-pattern self-audit if you run a platform.

steps.title: Source products: domestic clusters, B2B platforms or imports — with written specs and samples
steps.why: Margin is made at purchase. Clusters (Surat, Tirupur, Ludhiana, Moradabad, Jaipur, Agra, Noida) and B2B platforms give MOQs small brands can live with; imports need duty, BIS and label planning.
steps.how: Start with IndiaMART/TradeIndia/Udaan or a cluster visit; get samples, a signed spec sheet, GST invoices and a quality-check plan. For imports estimate landed cost (CIF + duty + IGST + freight + clearing) before you commit.

steps.title: Get the Importer-Exporter Code (IEC) from DGFT
steps.why: Customs will not clear a goods import or export without an IEC; it is also needed to claim export incentives and most banks ask for it on foreign receipts.
steps.how: Register on dgft.gov.in, Apply for IEC with PAN, bank certificate/cancelled cheque and address proof; pay ₹500; approval is usually same day. Update it every April–June even when nothing changed.

steps.title: Register your bank’s AD code at each port on ICEGATE
steps.why: Export shipping bills cannot be filed, and drawback/RoDTEP cannot be credited, until the Authorised Dealer code of your bank is registered at the port of export.
steps.how: Get the AD-code letter from your bank, create an ICEGATE account (IEC + DSC), submit the AD-code registration for each port/courier terminal you will use.

steps.title: Take RCMC from your Export Promotion Council (FIEO for multi-product)
steps.why: Needed to claim FTP benefits (advance authorisation, EPCG, MAI) and for many buyer programmes; councils also run subsidised trade fairs.
steps.how: Apply on DGFT’s e-RCMC module choosing the council for your product (APEDA food, EPCH handicrafts, AEPC apparel, GJEPC jewellery, Pharmexcil, SEPC services, FIEO general). Annual membership fee.

steps.title: Set up export documentation: proforma, commercial invoice, packing list, shipping bill, e-BRC
steps.why: Each shipment needs a clean paper trail for customs, the bank and GST refunds; e-BRC closes the loop proving the money came in.
steps.how: Template your invoice (IEC, GSTIN, LUT no., HS code, Incoterm, currency), packing list and declarations; your CHA or courier files the shipping bill marked for RoDTEP/drawback; after payment, self-certify the e-BRC on DGFT within the realisation window.

steps.title: Claim RoDTEP, duty drawback and ECGC cover
steps.why: RoDTEP refunds embedded taxes (0.5–4% of FOB) as transferable scrips; drawback refunds customs duty on inputs; ECGC insures against buyer default. Unclaimed money is the most common small-exporter mistake.
steps.how: Tick RoDTEP on the shipping bill, generate scrips on ICEGATE after scroll; drawback credits automatically to the AD-code bank; buy an ECGC policy for open-account buyers.

steps.title: Compute landed cost: BCD + 10% SWS + IGST on the total, plus freight, insurance and clearing
steps.why: Duty is charged on CIF value; IGST is charged on CIF plus duty. Mis-estimating by one slab can erase the margin on a container.
steps.how: Find the 8-digit ITC-HS, read BCD on the CBIC tariff, check anti-dumping/safeguard duties and FTA concessions (needs a certificate of origin), add 10% social welfare surcharge on BCD, then IGST (creditable) on the sum. Use the duty tool.

steps.title: Appoint a customs broker (CHA) and file the Bill of Entry; check restricted items and labelling
steps.why: Imports need a Bill of Entry, duty payment, and compliance with BIS, FSSAI (food), Legal Metrology labels (MRP stickers before clearance), drug/cosmetic rules and import policy restrictions.
steps.how: Share invoice, packing list, bill of lading/airway bill, COO and licences with the CHA; pay duty on ICEGATE; for e-commerce samples use courier (CSB-IV/V). Keep records 5 years.

steps.title: Software/IT exporters: register with STPI as a non-STP unit and file SOFTEX
steps.why: RBI requires software exported electronically to be declared on SOFTEX forms certified by STPI; banks increasingly ask for SOFTEX numbers before closing export receipts.
steps.how: Register as a non-STP unit at your STPI centre, then file SOFTEX for each invoice (or monthly) within 30 days of the invoice; match them to FIRAs at your bank.
steps.cost: Annual service charge by export slab (₹1,000–30,000+)

steps.title: Issue offer letters and employment contracts with IP assignment and confidentiality
steps.why: Without an IP-assignment clause, code and designs made by employees may not belong to the company — a diligence red flag.
steps.how: Use a standard contract: role, CTC with the 50%-wages rule of the Labour Codes in mind, probation, notice, confidentiality, IP assignment, POSH policy acknowledgement. Fixed-term staff now earn gratuity pro-rata after one year.

steps.title: Register for professional tax (PTEC/PTRC) where your state levies it
steps.why: Maharashtra, Karnataka, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Telangana, Andhra, MP, Odisha and others tax salaries up to ₹2,500 a year; the employer deducts and remits monthly. Delhi, UP, Haryana and Rajasthan do not levy it.
steps.how: Enrol the entity (PTEC) and register as employer (PTRC) on the state commercial tax portal; deduct from salaries; file monthly/annual returns.
steps.cost: ₹2,500 a year for the entity + employee deductions

steps.title: Register with EPFO (20+ employees) and ESIC (10+ employees, wages ≤ ₹21,000)
steps.why: Coverage is mandatory once headcount crosses the threshold and continues even if it drops later; late registration means back-contributions with damages.
steps.how: Register on Shram Suvidha / EPFO employer portal and ESIC with incorporation proof, PAN, address proof, employee list and bank details; file monthly ECR by the 15th. Many startups register voluntarily earlier because employees ask for PF.
steps.cost: EPF 12% + 0.5% EDLI + admin; ESI 3.25% of wages

steps.title: Adopt a POSH policy and form an Internal Committee at 10 employees
steps.why: The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act requires a policy, an Internal Committee with an external member, awareness sessions and an annual report; non-compliance is a fine and a licence-cancellation ground.
steps.how: Adopt a written policy, constitute the IC (presiding woman officer, two employees, one external NGO/legal member), display the order, train staff, file the annual report with the District Officer.

steps.title: Run payroll: salary TDS (section 192), Form 16, labour-code wage structure
steps.why: Employers must deduct tax monthly on estimated annual salary, deposit by the 7th, file quarterly 24Q and issue Form 16 by 15 June.
steps.how: Collect investment declarations and regime choice from staff, compute TDS monthly, deposit via the income-tax portal, file 24Q quarterly on TRACES, maintain registers (wages, attendance, leave) under the Codes.

steps.title: Set up a foreign entity the FEMA-compliant way (ODI via your AD bank, Form FC)
steps.why: An Indian resident or company owning a Delaware LLC or Singapore Pte Ltd — even with zero cash — is Overseas Direct Investment under the 2022 rules and must be reported through an AD bank, get a UIN and file an Annual Performance Report.
steps.how: Decide the structure (India parent with foreign subsidiary vs. a ‘flip’ to a foreign parent). Route funds under LRS (individuals, within US$250k) or ODI (company, up to 400% of net worth) with Form FC through the bank within 30 days; keep two layers of subsidiaries maximum; file APR every December and FLA every July.

steps.title: Taking money from foreign investors: pricing, FC-GPR within 30 days, sector caps
steps.why: Shares issued to non-residents must be at or above fair value (merchant-banker/CA valuation), reported in FC-GPR on RBI FIRMS within 30 days of allotment, and respect sectoral caps (e-commerce marketplace 100% automatic; inventory e-commerce and multi-brand retail restricted).
steps.how: Create the Entity Master on FIRMS, get a valuation report, receive funds with a FIRC and KYC of the investor, allot within 60 days, file FC-GPR. Investors from land-border countries need government approval (Press Note 3 of 2020).

steps.title: Get ready for the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (full force 13 May 2027)
steps.why: Any business that collects names, phones, emails or payment data is a Data Fiduciary: itemised consent notices, purpose limitation, breach reporting within 72 hours, deletion when the purpose ends, verifiable parental consent for under-18s. Penalties run to ₹250 crore.
steps.how: Map what personal data you collect and where it goes (analytics, payment gateways, CRMs); rewrite the privacy notice; log consents; set retention; write a breach plan; name a contact for grievances (respond within 90 days).

steps.title: Keep double-entry books with an audit trail from day one
steps.why: Companies must use software with an edit log; GST reconciliation (GSTR-2B vs purchases) and tax audits are impossible without clean books; investors’ diligence starts here.
steps.how: Record every sale, purchase, expense and bank entry monthly in Zoho Books/Tally/Vyapar; reconcile bank statements monthly; store invoices and vouchers 8 years (companies), 72 months (GST), 6 years (income tax).

steps.title: File GST returns: GSTR-1 (11th), GSTR-3B (20th) or quarterly under QRMP; GSTR-9 by 31 December
steps.why: Late fees accrue daily, input credit depends on suppliers filing on time, and returns older than three years can no longer be filed at all.
steps.how: Reconcile sales with your books and e-invoices, accept/reject supplier invoices in IMS, claim credit only from GSTR-2B, pay by the 20th (or 22nd/24th quarterly). Annual return if turnover exceeds ₹2 crore; GSTR-9C above ₹5 crore.

steps.title: Deduct and deposit TDS by the 7th; file 24Q/26Q quarterly; issue certificates
steps.why: Paying rent above ₹50,000/month, contractors, professionals, commission or salaries without deducting tax disallows 30% of the expense and brings interest and penalties.
steps.how: Know the common sections and thresholds (rent 194-I ₹2.4 lakh/yr; contractors 194C ₹30,000 per bill/₹1 lakh per year; professionals 194J ₹50,000; commission 194H ₹20,000), deposit monthly, file quarterly returns on TRACES, download and issue Form 16/16A.

steps.title: Pay advance tax in four instalments (15 Jun, 15 Sep, 15 Dec, 15 Mar)
steps.why: If your tax for the year exceeds ₹10,000 you must pay as you earn; presumptive taxpayers pay once by 15 March. Shortfalls carry 1% monthly interest.
steps.how: Estimate profit each quarter, pay 15/45/75/100% cumulatively through the e-filing portal (challan 280). Companies and LLPs always; proprietors unless senior citizens without business income.

steps.title: File the income-tax return (ITR-3/4 proprietors, ITR-5 firms/LLPs, ITR-6 companies)
steps.why: Due 31 July (no audit), 31 October (audit cases and companies), 30 November (transfer pricing). Late filing costs up to ₹5,000 and forfeits loss carry-forward.
steps.how: Close the books, get the tax audit report uploaded by 30 September where applicable, reconcile with AIS/26AS, file and e-verify. Under the 2025 Act the ‘tax year’ replaces previous/assessment year language — the deadlines are unchanged.

steps.title: Appoint an auditor (ADT-1) and get the statutory audit done every year
steps.why: Every company, however small, must have its accounts audited by a Chartered Accountant; the first auditor is appointed within 30 days of incorporation.
steps.how: Board appoints the first auditor within 30 days (members at the first AGM for five years, file ADT-1 within 15 days of the AGM). Hand over books by June; audited financials go to the AGM by 30 September.

steps.title: ROC annual filings: AGM by 30 Sep, AOC-4 within 30 days, MGT-7/7A within 60 days, DIR-3 KYC by 30 Sep, DPT-3 by 30 Jun, MSME-1 half-yearly
steps.why: Each late form costs ₹100 per day with no cap, and directors whose KYC lapses get their DIN deactivated.
steps.how: Hold the AGM (OPCs exempt), file financials (AOC-4) and the annual return (MGT-7A for small companies), each director files DIR-3 KYC, report deposits/loans in DPT-3 and overdue MSME payables in MSME-1 (30 Apr, 31 Oct). Keep minutes and statutory registers.
steps.cost: MCA fees ₹200–600 per form + CS/CA fees

steps.title: LLP annual filings: Form 11 by 30 May, Form 8 by 30 October; audit above ₹40 lakh turnover or ₹25 lakh contribution
steps.why: LLPs skip AGMs and most registers, but the two annual forms are mandatory with ₹100/day late fees; designated partners also file DIR-3 KYC.
steps.how: Form 11 (annual return of partners) by 30 May; Form 8 (statement of accounts and solvency) by 30 October, audited if over the limits; income-tax return by 31 July or 31 October.

steps.title: Hold board meetings (small companies: two a year, 90 days apart) and keep minutes and registers
steps.why: Resolutions for bank accounts, loans, share allotments and ESOPs must be minuted; investors and auditors will ask for the minute book.
steps.how: Calendar two board meetings (four for non-small companies) plus the AGM; keep registers of members, directors, charges and contracts; minutes signed within 30 days.

steps.title: Renew what expires: IEC update (Apr–Jun), LUT (Apr), FSSAI, trade licence, Shops & Establishment, DSCs, trademark (10 years)
steps.why: Lapsed registrations are discovered at the worst time — at customs, at a marketplace audit, or when a licence inspector visits.
steps.how: Put renewal dates in the compliance calendar; most renew online in minutes if done before expiry and cost multiples if late.

steps.title: Pay Udyam-registered suppliers within 45 days (and chase your own buyers under the MSMED Act)
steps.why: Payments to micro and small suppliers beyond 45 days are disallowed as expenses until paid (s.43B(h) regime continued in the 2025 Act) and carry compound interest at three times the bank rate; as a supplier you can file on MSME Samadhaan.
steps.how: Tag Udyam suppliers in your accounting software, pay within the agreed term (max 45 days), report overdue amounts in MSME-1 if you are a company; file Samadhaan claims against slow buyers.
